steps.observation: You have 300 seconds. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Here are the major ways in which RNA (ribonucleic acid) and DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) differ:

1. Sugar Moiety  
   • DNA contains deoxyribose, which lacks an oxygen atom on the 2′ carbon.  
   • RNA contains ribose, which has a hydroxyl (–OH) group on the 2′ carbon.  
   – The extra –OH in RNA makes it more chemically reactive and less stable than DNA.

2. Nitrogenous Bases  
   • DNA uses adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C), and thymine (T).  
   • RNA uses adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C), and uracil (U) in place of thymine.  
   – Thymine has a methyl group that uracil lacks; this methylation helps protect DNA from damage.

3. Strandedness and Structure  
   • DNA is most commonly found as a long, stable, double-stranded helix (the famous Watson-Crick double helix).  
   • RNA is usually single-stranded and can fold into complex three-dimensional shapes (hairpins, loops, bulges).  
   – Some RNAs (e.g., certain viruses) can be double-stranded or form transient duplexes during function.

4. Location in the Cell  
   • DNA resides primarily in the cell nucleus (eukaryotes), and in mitochondria or chloroplasts.  
   • RNA is synthesized in the nucleus but functions throughout the cell: in the cytoplasm, ribosomes, and various organelles.

5. Primary Biological Roles  
   • DNA is the long-term repository of genetic information—it carries the instructions for building and maintaining an organism.  
   • RNA serves multiple roles:  
     – Messenger RNA (mRNA) carries genetic code from DNA to ribosomes.  
     – Transfer RNA (tRNA) delivers amino acids during protein synthesis.  
     – Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) is a structural and enzymatic component of ribosomes.  
     – Regulatory RNAs (e.g., microRNA, siRNA, lncRNA) control gene expression and other processes.

6. Stability and Lifespan  
   • DNA is relatively stable—degradation is slow under cellular conditions. This stability makes it ideal for long-term information storage.  
   • RNA is more prone to hydrolysis (due to the 2′-OH) and generally has a shorter half-life, allowing dynamic regulation of gene expression.

7. Chemical Modifications  
   • DNA can be methylated (e.g., 5-methylcytosine) for epigenetic regulation.  
   • RNA undergoes a variety of modifications (e.g., 5′ cap, poly-A tail, pseudouridine, methylations) that affect its processing, stability, and function.

Summary  
DNA is a deoxyribose-based, double-stranded, stable molecule dedicated to long-term storage of genetic information. RNA is a ribose-based, usually single-stranded, more reactive molecule that plays diverse roles in decoding, regulating, and executing the instructions encoded by DNA.
